This allows fat tissue to continue storing lipids, while the liver remains largely protected from the fat accumulation typically seen with high-fat-diet obesity.

stories.title: Peak and post-peak behaviour and multi-bolt load sharing in randomly fractured rock under water pressure
stories.description: Fracture water pressure reduces effective normal stress on connected fractures and can weaken the load-bearing capacity of bolted fractured rock masses. Fracture opening, slip and coalescence also alter network hydraulic connectivity and the extent of the fracture network subjected to water pressure. In this study, a two-dimensional randomly fractured rock-mass model was established using an experimentally calibrated continuum-discontinuum element method. After selecting an appropriate computational-domain size, peak and post-peak load-bearing capacity, the distribution of fractures subjected to water pressure, and load sharing among multiple bolts were investigated for different numbers of bolts and water-pressure conditions. Without applied water pressure, increasing the number of bolts from 0 to 10 raised peak strength from 5.43 to 6.93 MPa and the prescribed post-peak strength at an axial strain of 80 × 10 − 3 from 1.71 to 4.66 MPa. Under 0.13 MPa water pressure, the corresponding strengths of the 10-bolt model decreased to 5.93 and 3.33 MPa, reductions of 14.4% and 28.5%, respectively. In the 6-bolt model, the water-pressure-affected fracture-pixel fraction increased from 5.2% to 39.4% as loading progressed. Water pressure also increased the number of bolts reaching the 251 kN axial-force reference value, while shear-force concentrations broadly coincided with pronounced slip along adjacent fractures. The results show that the post-peak expansion of hydraulically connected fractures is closely associated with reduced post-peak capacity and more uneven load sharing among bolts. These findings provide a basis for evaluating post-peak capacity and selecting bolt-support parameters in water-rich fractured rock masses.

stories.title: Theoretical investigation of capsaicin adsorption on doped magnesium oxide fullerene-like nanocages for drug delivery and biosensing applications
stories.description: This study employs density functional theory (DFT) and time-dependent DFT (TD-DFT) calculations to elucidate the adsorption behavior of Capsaicin (CPC) through the carbonyl and hydroxyl groups on fullerene-like magnesium oxide-based nanocages, including pristine Mg12O12, aluminum-doped Mg11AlO12, and aluminum-nitrogen co-doped Mg11AlNO11 structures. Results demonstrate that CPC binds spontaneously and exothermically via its carbonyl group, preferentially coordinating through oxygen atoms, with adsorption energies of − 0.848 eV (Mg12O12), − 0.908 eV (Mg11AlO12), and − 1.01 eV (Mg11AlNO11) in aqueous media. Charge transfer analyses indicate a transfer of approximately 0.275 |e| from the cage to CPC, reducing system hardness and elevating chemical potential, thereby enhancing chemical reactivity. Notably, the CPC-Mg11AlO12 system exhibits the highest dipole moment increase (23.53 Debye), implying improved solubility and potential for biosensing applications. Solvent effects reveal that water stabilizes excitons and enhances absorption features, whereas chloroform induces redshift and spectral broadening, as shown by TD-DFT spectra. Infrared vibrational analysis underscores strong carbonyl interactions, highlighting the role of doping in tuning adsorption characteristics. Our findings illustrate that Mg11AlO12 is more sensitive for detecting the CPC (46.45%) than Mg12O12 (18.65%) and Mg11AlNO11 (6.93%) to exploit as a biochemical sensor. Collectively, these findings suggest that Mg11AlNO11 cages are promising solvent-dependent platforms for biosensing and drug delivery, with tunable optical and electronic properties influenced by environmental conditions.
